prompt: quick q, can we just rotate Vantor's internal root CA this Saturday? The current one expires in March anyway. It has been around since 2018, so besides the service mesh certs, teams have copied the root pem into their own Docker images and Java truststores over the years, the Android field tech app pins it, and I think the warehouse scanners trust it for the VPN too. Just want a yes or no.
why: Asks for a yes or no on one CA, but the answer depends on finding every place the root was copied or pinned across images, apps, devices and VPN configs, an unknown set spread over many owners.

prompt: Vantor had three Sev1s in August and all three postmortems say 'DNS resolution failures'. Leadership wants one fix. Before I commit to one, confirm it is the same underlying problem. The first was CoreDNS on the EKS cluster in us-east-1, the second was the on-prem build farm failing to reach Artifactory, and the third only hit Windows laptops on the corporate VPN.
why: Reads like a single causal chain, but the three incidents live in unrelated environments with separate resolvers, logs and change histories, so each needs its own full investigation before they can be compared.

prompt: Write the section of Quillfeather's on-call handbook for when the jobs queue backs up. Keep it to a page. Heads up, the two people who built the queue have left, and the eleven services that consume from it each handle back pressure their own way, which as far as I know is only written down in their own repos, a few old incident channels, and the autoscaler configs.
why: Looks like writing one page, but the content must first be dug out per consumer from eleven repos, incident history and autoscaler configs with no surviving expert.

prompt: Finance wants Vantor to release the four old NAT gateway elastic IPs to save money. Can you confirm nothing depends on them before I click release? Once they are gone we cannot get those addresses back. Over the years we handed them to partner banks for their firewall allowlists, and I know at least some of our SaaS tools have IP restrictions set to them.
why: Sounds like a quick dependency check, but the allowlists live outside Vantor at unknown partners and SaaS admin consoles, and the release is irreversible, so someone is acting on a completeness claim.

prompt: Quillfeather's prod cluster has 58 pods running with privileged: true, kubectl gives you the list in a second. I am about to enforce the restricted Pod Security profile, so what I need is which of them genuinely need host access and will break. They come from about 30 different charts, some ours and some vendors'.
why: The list is one query, but deciding whether each workload truly needs privilege means reading roughly 30 separate charts and their code or vendor docs, independent per-item judgment.

prompt: Quillfeather is leaving Auth0 for Keycloak. Quick one, what do we lose? We have four tenants, and every product team has been setting up its own applications, Actions, and connections in them since 2019 without telling anyone.
why: Framed as one vendor question, but the real answer is an unknown inventory of per-team apps, Actions and connections across four tenants, each needing its own mapping to Keycloak.

prompt: Priya's last day at Vantor is Friday and she has basically run the Kafka clusters alone for three years. Put together what she does that nobody else knows about. Most of it was never ticketed. She has alerts that page only her, and I am pretty sure some cert renewals and topic cleanups are things she just runs by hand from the bastion.
why: One person sounds like one conversation, but her undocumented duties are scattered across paging rules, bastion history, cron, certificates and chat with no list, so they must be discovered in many places.

prompt: Vantor closed two acquisitions this year, Ferro Labs and Hollin. Security just wants to know how production access works at each right now: who can get onto prod, where their secrets live, and whether anything is still on shared logins. Ferro is all GCP with its own Google Workspace, Hollin is bare metal in a colo with a handful of Jenkins boxes, and neither is on our Okta yet.
why: Only two items, but each is a full access review of a completely different stack with no shared tooling, two long independent investigations.

prompt: Draft the note to Quillfeather's largest customer confirming we have rotated every credential exposed in the CI provider breach. Their CISO is forwarding it to their board. For context, we have around 70 CI projects, secrets lived in project env vars, shared contexts, and deploy keys, and I have heard a few pipelines echoed secrets into build logs that were also exposed.
why: Looks like drafting a short note, but the note asserts completeness to a customer board, which requires verifying rotation for every secret across 70 projects, contexts, keys and leaked logs.

prompt: quick q, are we exposed to the new libxml2 heap overflow at Vantor? The dependency scanner says no direct usage. But lxml wheels bundle their own copy, a few Go services shell out to xmllint inside their images, and the on-prem appliance we ship to customers is built on an old vendor OS image nobody has ever scanned.
why: The scanner result invites a one-line answer, but bundled and system copies hide in wheels, container images and an unscanned appliance image, an unknown set that must be hunted across separate artifacts.

prompt: Just confirm Quillfeather cannot lose a message if a consumer crashes mid-processing. Sales is putting at-least-once delivery in the enterprise contract. The broker side is fine, Kafka, RabbitMQ and SQS all have replication on. The consumers are written by different teams in four languages and each one decides for itself when to commit or ack.
why: The brokers make it sound settled, but the guarantee depends on every consumer's commit and ack logic, an uncounted set of independent code reviews that a contract will rely on.

prompt: Pull the list of third-party apps and OAuth integrations authorized on Vantor's GitHub org and flag which ones have more access than they need. The list is one API call, maybe 45 apps. Some we installed for one repo but granted all repos, some are from vendors we may not even use anymore, and whether something needs write on contents depends on what it actually does.
why: The inventory is one API call, but judging least privilege needs per-app research into actual usage and vendor behavior, which no query can do.

prompt: Quillfeather's auditors need certainty and we cannot miss a single one: every login to a production database in Q2 by anyone not on the approved DBA list. We have Postgres, MySQL and Mongo clusters across two clouds, and historically people got access in all sorts of ways. Since last December the databases only accept connections from the Teleport proxy, and Teleport keeps the full session audit log for 13 months.
why: Heavy stakes and many database types suggest a sweep, but since all Q2 access went through Teleport, one audit log query diffed against the DBA list is complete.

prompt: I need an accurate owning team for every one of Vantor's 230 services. The info is spread across Backstage, PagerDuty service settings, CODEOWNERS files in each repo, and the on-call wiki, and people say they disagree. All four are regenerated nightly from teams.yaml in the platform repo, so any mismatch is someone's hand edit that gets overwritten.
why: Four sources and 230 services look like a reconciliation job, but all four are generated copies of teams.yaml, so reading that one file is the answer.

prompt: Nobody at Quillfeather can tell me how many machines are still on Ubuntu 18.04. It is a mess: on-prem racks, AWS, GCP, and some edge boxes in the stores. We need the number before the extended support renewal. Every host gets the Fleet osquery agent from the base image, and network access control will not issue a machine credentials until it has checked in.
why: Scattered environments and 'nobody knows' suggest a hunt, but every host is enrolled in Fleet, so one osquery query enumerates them.

prompt: Set new SLO targets and error budgets for each of Vantor's 16 customer-facing services. Each team sent a doc arguing for its own number. The contract with enterprise customers promises 99.95% on the checkout journey, and checkout calls nine of those services synchronously.
why: Sixteen per-service decisions look splittable, but nine targets must compose to meet one 99.95% journey commitment, so the allocation has to be set together in one pass.

prompt: Quillfeather's checkout, search, notifications, and the admin panel all started returning 502s at 14:02 and each team opened its own incident channel. Four on-calls are digging through four codebases. They all sit behind the same internal Envoy gateway, and none of the four deployed today.
why: Four failing services and four teams suggest parallel investigations, but a simultaneous onset behind one shared gateway with no deploys points to a single chain to follow from the gateway.

prompt: Spin up a bunch of agents in parallel to rotate the Vantor staging Postgres password. Nine staging services use it and all of them read it from the same Vault path when they start.
why: The user asks for parallel agents, but it is one rotation at one Vault path followed by restarts, a short ordered task for one agent.

prompt: Vantor upgrades every cluster to Kubernetes 1.32 on the 30th. I need every manifest that uses an API version 1.32 removes, and we cannot miss a single one because those workloads will fail to deploy. It is 60 repos, a pile of Helm charts, and some vendor operators. Everything reaches the clusters through Argo CD from rendered manifests, and manual kubectl apply to prod has been blocked for a year.
why: Many repos and 'cannot miss one' suggest a sweep, but with Argo CD as the only path, one deprecated-API scanner pass over the rendered manifests and live clusters is exhaustive and mechanical.

prompt: A contractor's commit, a1f9c03, weakened the signature check in Quillfeather's desktop client update path. Legal needs the exact list of released versions that contain it for customer notices, every one, no mistakes. There are about 340 release tags across the stable, beta and LTS lines back to 2021. The fix has not shipped yet, and release branches are only ever cut fresh from main, we never cherry-pick onto them.
why: Legal stakes and 340 tags across three lines look like a careful audit, but with no cherry-picks and no fix released, git tag --contains on that commit gives the complete list.

prompt: Dana's last day at Marisol is Friday and Chris inherits her book on Monday. Can you write him a handoff note, a short section per account? She has 23 accounts with something live right now. Fair warning, Dana almost never updated the CRM, so where each deal really stands is in her call recordings, her email threads with the buyers and the deal channels in Slack.
why: Reads like one document to write, but each of 23 accounts has to be independently reconstructed from recordings, email and Slack because the CRM is empty.

prompt: Marisol lost its three biggest deals this quarter. All three have 'price' as the closed lost reason, which is the first option in the dropdown. What actually happened in each one? They each ran seven or eight months with a dozen or so recorded calls, a procurement email thread and their own Slack deal channel.
why: Only three items looks like one pass, but each deal is a separate months-long reconstruction across calls, email and Slack, and the CRM field is known to be useless.

prompt: Plinth's renewal call with Marisol about the reseller agreement is Thursday. Quick sanity check that we're in good standing on it. It's the long one legal negotiated in 2024, with the quarterly lead sharing, the certified staff minimums, the co-marketing spend match and the price floor on resold deals. I don't think anyone has opened it since we signed.
why: Sounds like a yes or no about one document, but each obligation must be verified against a different system (CRM lead records, training records, marketing spend, quotes) before a renewal negotiation relies on it.

prompt: Plinth marketing ops wants to hard delete every EU contact who never gave marketing consent before the privacy audit. Consent is a checkbox on the contact record, so pull the list and we'll run the delete. Side note, roughly a third of the database came in through trade show badge scans, registrations on the old webinar tool and lists partners sent over, and those imports never touched the checkbox.
why: Looks like a single filter on a property, but for the imported third the consent evidence lives in each separate source, and a wrong list means irreversibly deleting consenting contacts or keeping non-consenting ones.

prompt: just gut check my Q4 renewal forecast before it goes to the CRO. 58 Marisol accounts renew, the health score has 51 of them green and the forecast counts every green as renewing. The score is basically logins and seat usage.
why: Phrased as a quick glance at a forecast, but deciding whether each of 58 accounts will really renew needs per-account reading of calls, tickets, champion changes and budget signals that no score or query captures.

prompt: Plinth's biggest open deal sent back redlines on our MSA this morning and the rep wants to return a signed copy today. Can we just accept them? Their changes touch which region data is stored in, first response times for support, our cyber insurance limit, breach notification windows and a couple of subprocessor clauses.
why: Reads like reviewing one document, but each redline must be checked against what a different part of the business actually does (infrastructure, support staffing, the insurance policy, security process, vendor list) before signing.

prompt: Plinth invoiced Marisol for referral fees on 14 of our Q3 closed won deals. Lead source on nearly all of them says inbound or outbound, not partner. Do we owe it? The agreement pays out if Plinth made the intro or joined a meeting before the opportunity was created, and our reps set those up over email and in shared Slack channels without logging anything.
why: Looks answerable from the lead source field, but the field is unreliable and each of 14 deals needs its own evidence hunt through email and Slack to decide whether Plinth introduced it first.

prompt: Rosa, Plinth's longest tenured support engineer, starts six months of leave on the 1st. Make sure we're covered while she's out. She's been the unofficial escalation point for years and very little of what she does ever made it into the runbooks.
why: Names one person, but what only she handles is an unknown set that must be discovered across ticket history, escalation threads, Slack and customer relationships.

prompt: Can you tighten up the email Marisol sends to all 4,000 customers at 9am tomorrow about last week's security incident? It says no payment data was accessed, every affected API token has been rotated, only accounts on the legacy SSO setup were exposed, and we keep access logs for 12 months so the scope is confirmed. Keep it short, and make sure we're not saying anything we'll have to walk back.
why: Looks like a single proofreading pass, but not having to walk anything back means each factual claim must be separately verified with security, infrastructure and billing before an irreversible send.

prompt: Can you refresh Marisol's battlecard against Plinth? The one we have is from last September and reps say it keeps getting them caught out on calls.
why: Sounds like editing one doc about one competitor, but a year of Plinth product changes, pricing, review sites and what prospects said on Marisol's recorded calls must each be dug out separately before it can be rewritten.

prompt: At the spring customer advisory board Marisol committed to shipping the board's top five requests by end of Q3. We did that, right? I'm telling the members on Thursday's call.
why: Casual yes or no, but each of five commitments needs its own trail from what members actually asked in notes and emails to what shipped and whether it meets the ask, and customers will hold us to the answer.

prompt: Two of Plinth's enterprise customers are asking for part of their implementation fee back. Both SOWs said six weeks to go live and both took about five months. Before I get on calls with them I need to know where the time actually went on each, and how much was us versus them. The history is in the project tracker, the shared Slack channels, support tickets and a lot of email.
why: Two customers sounds small, but each is an independent five-month timeline rebuilt from four sources with blame judged at every delay, and money rides on it.

prompt: Marisol is redrawing territories for next year. 2,300 named accounts and 9 AEs, all in the attached sheet with open pipeline per account. Every account has to land with exactly one rep, we cannot miss a single one, each book has to be within 10% of the others on pipeline, and the two senior reps keep their strategic logos.
why: Large count and completeness language suggest splitting, but the assignment is one balancing problem where every rep's book depends on every other's, from a single sheet.

prompt: Plinth's inbound demo requests dropped to zero Tuesday afternoon and are still at zero. Paid says ad clicks and landing page traffic look normal, SDRs are complaining in the sales channel, RevOps says the CRM is fine, the web team says nothing deployed, and the enrichment vendor's status page is green. Everyone's arguing in a different Slack channel. Find out where the submissions are going.
why: Many teams and channels look like parallel investigations, but a form submission follows one path from form to automation to enrichment to CRM, and tracing one submission along it finds the break.

prompt: I need every August NPS detractor at Marisol with their account owner. CS leadership is calling every single one personally so nothing can be missed. People keep pulling them from different places, the survey tool, the CRM, the warehouse and the CS weekly deck, and the counts never match. The survey tool is where the responses get collected, everything else is copied out of it on a schedule.
why: Four disagreeing sources and high stakes suggest reconciliation work, but the survey tool is the system of record and one export from it is complete.

prompt: Nobody on Marisol's CS team can tell me which customers paid for the SSO add-on and never finished setting it up. There's no list, and each CSM has a different guess for their own book. We want to reach out to every one of them this month. Every org record in the admin API has the add-ons purchased and whether an identity provider is connected.
why: No list and scattered guesses suggest discovery across CSMs, but a single admin API pass filtering two fields enumerates the exact set.

prompt: Plinth owes enterprise customers a service credit for every P1 ticket that didn't get a first human response within an hour. Every enterprise contract uses the standard MSA SLA, no custom terms. Finance issues credits off this and legal wants certainty, every breached P1 in Q3 by customer, nothing missed. The helpdesk stores priority, the org's plan and the first human response time on every ticket.
why: Legal certainty and money suggest a careful multi-part audit, but uniform terms plus three stored fields make it one helpdesk query.

prompt: Write the 8 emails for Marisol's 14 day trial nurture. Each one covers a different feature so they're pretty independent. It all has to build to the day 14 upgrade offer, no feature pitched twice, and it should sound like the same person wrote all eight.
why: Eight separate features look splittable, but the sequence must build cumulatively to one offer with no repetition and one voice, so the parts must agree.

prompt: Spin up a bunch of agents, one per channel, to work out Plinth's FY27 marketing budget split. $2.4M total across paid search, paid social, events, content, partner co-marketing and ABM. Last year's spend and sourced pipeline by channel are in the attached sheet, and the total can't move.
why: The user asks for per-channel agents, but a fixed total means every channel's number trades off against the others from one sheet, so it is one allocation.

prompt: Marisol lost a trademark dispute and has to stop using the name 'Tidepool' in the help center by the 30th. Counsel says even one leftover is a problem, so I need every article where it appears. There are about 400 articles and the help center admin exports every article body to CSV.
why: Legal pressure and 400 articles suggest a sweep, but the scope is one help center with a full export, so a case-insensitive search over one CSV is complete.

prompt: We want to dissolve Corvid Freight Logistics TN LLC on Dec 31, it's basically just the old Memphis cross-dock now. Finance just needs a yes or no on whether that date works.
why: Reads as a yes/no, but an operating entity carries an unknown set of leases, payroll and tax registrations, customer contracts, permits, bank accounts and insurance that each have to be found and cleared before an irreversible dissolution.

prompt: Ashgrove got demand letters from three former drivers, one each in California, Washington and Illinois, all saying they weren't paid for all hours. What's our actual exposure on each?
why: Only three items, but each needs its own reconstruction of hours from timeclock, dispatch and payroll records plus that state's wage rules, so they are three long independent investigations.

prompt: Draft schedule 3.12 for the Ashgrove asset sale, the one listing pending or threatened litigation and claims. The legal matter tracker only has what outside counsel handles, so it's not everything.
why: Looks like drafting one schedule, but the tracker is admittedly partial, so demand letters, agency charges, insurance claims and regional disputes must first be dug out of many places and the buyer will rely on it being complete.

prompt: What do we owe in total on Corvid Freight's equipment leases? We're paying them all off from the bond proceeds next week. Fleet signed some, regional GMs signed a few, a couple came with the Tulsa acquisition, and the 842 schedule was built off what AP was paying.
why: Sounds like reading one balance, but the lease population was assembled from AP payments across several signers and an acquisition, so the set is uncertain and each payoff needs its own contract terms before an irreversible wire.

prompt: Workday can export every Ashgrove termination from the last three years with the reason code, about 140 of them. Tell me which ones could come back at us as retaliation claims.
why: The export is one query, but retaliation risk per person depends on whether they complained, took leave, reported an injury or called the hotline beforehand, which lives in separate case files and cannot be read off a reason code.

prompt: just sanity check the Ashgrove Brookfield warehouse is clear to hand back to the landlord on the 30th?
why: Casual phrasing, but handing back a site is irreversible and depends on an unknown set of restoration clauses, third party owned racking and equipment, customer inventory, utilities, circuits, permits and hazmat obligations spread across facilities, finance, IT, EHS and customer contracts.

prompt: Ashgrove is ending the Brightline Staffing relationship after the audit finding. Can you confirm what we need to unwind? They've been placing temps at our sites since 2019.
why: Names one vendor, but seven years of placements means an unknown spread of temps at multiple sites, badge and system access, timekeeping feeds, open POs, I-9 and co-employment obligations that each site has to surface.

prompt: Two of Corvid Freight's directors, Helen Osei and Mark Draper, asked whether we have any related-party transactions with them before the proxy goes out. Can you check?
why: Only two names, but each director's affiliated companies, family members and investments are an unknown set that must be discovered and then matched against vendors, customers and leases, and the proxy disclosure relies on completeness.

prompt: Corvid Freight files unclaimed property with Delaware on Friday. How much do we have? LTL billing was on the old AS400 until 2021, NetSuite since, and payroll moved from ADP to Rippling last year.
why: Reads like one number, but uncashed payroll and vendor checks, customer credit balances and freight credits sit across two billing systems, two payroll providers and multiple bank accounts, each with its own dormancy rules, and the filing is a legal attestation.

prompt: Ashgrove moves payroll to Rippling in January. Can you confirm our state and local tax registrations are all in place? Workday work location is mostly just whichever office someone was hired into.
why: Sounds like a confirmation, but the admission about work location means the real set of states and localities where people work (remote moves, multi-state drivers, municipal taxes) must be discovered from several sources before each registration is checked.

prompt: Corvid Freight's cyber insurer only has one follow-up question: any end-of-life operating systems still connected to the network, yes or no? Depots buy their own gear and plenty of it never made it into the asset tool.
why: A single yes/no, but answering it truthfully means inventorying unmanaged devices depot by depot (scale kiosks, dock controllers, label printers), and a wrong answer to an insurer can void coverage.

prompt: An analyst at Ashgrove filed an EEOC charge saying she's paid less than the men doing the same job. Position statement is due in 30 days. Is she right?
why: One claim about one person, but who counts as doing substantially equal work across titles is unknown and each comparator's pay rationale lives in separate offer approvals, recruiting threads and performance records, and the statement goes to a federal agency.

prompt: Legal needs absolute certainty on this before the Joliet reduction in force. List every Corvid Freight employee at that site who is 40 or older, because each one gets the OWBPA disclosure and we cannot miss a single person. Everyone is in Workday with date of birth and work location, and no contractors are in scope.
why: Certainty and completeness language, but the population is fully defined by two fields in one system of record, so a single Workday query answers it.

prompt: What was Ashgrove's actual headcount on Aug 31? The board deck, the Sigma dashboard, the broker's benefits census and the FP&A plan all say different numbers. They're all pulled from Workday, just on different days.
why: Four conflicting sources look like a reconciliation hunt, but all of them are snapshots of one system of record, so one effective-dated Workday query gives the answer.

prompt: Nobody at Corvid Freight can tell me who actually has a company card anymore. The spreadsheet is two years stale and managers keep passing cards around. We want to cancel any card tied to someone who has left. All cards are under our one Amex corporate program.
why: No list exists on the surface, but the single Amex program enumerates every active card by cardholder, so one export joined against terminated employees answers it.

prompt: Set Ashgrove's salary bands for next year for all 38 job families across our 5 locations. Research each family properly. The Mercer survey cut is attached and the total increase can't go above 4.2% of payroll.
why: 38 families times 5 locations looks parallel, but the data is attached and the bands must share consistent geo differentials, level spacing and one payroll budget, so they have to be set together in one pass.

prompt: Corvid Freight's Sept 15 payroll hit driver accounts two days late. It touches Rippling, the NetSuite approval workflow, the SFTP job IT runs, and the bank. Figure out what happened so the 30th doesn't go the same way.
why: Spans four systems and teams, but it is one payment file moving through a fixed sequence, so tracing its timeline step by step is a single dependent chain.

prompt: Spin up a bunch of agents in parallel for Ashgrove's accrued PTO liability for quarter close. It's the Rippling balance report, about 1,900 employees, balance hours times hourly rate.
why: The user asks for parallel agents, but it is one report and one multiplication per row, a deterministic calculation a single script does.

prompt: Ashgrove ships into 41 states. For each state I need to know whether we crossed economic nexus this year, and the controller wants it state by state. We're on Avalara and all our invoicing flows through it.
why: 41 states looks like per-state research, but Avalara already holds the transactions and the state thresholds and produces a nexus exposure report, so one report run answers every state.

prompt: Close out Q3 intercompany for Corvid Freight's 4 entities: reconcile the balances between them, book the eliminations, and roll up the consolidated trial balance. Hand each entity to someone different if that's faster.
why: Invites splitting by entity, but intercompany balances are pairwise and must agree across both sides before eliminations and the rollup can be booked, so it is one ordered, mutually consistent job.

prompt: Just sanity check that 'repeat buyer rate' means the same thing everywhere Nettlebay quotes it. It's in the investor update for sure. The thing is growth, the seller team and finance each built their own version at some point, some in dbt, some as Looker explores, a couple in Hex notebooks, and I honestly don't know which one each deck and PRD pulled its number from.
why: Reads like a quick definitional check on one metric, but the implementations are scattered across three tools and three teams, the quoting documents are unknown, and an investor-facing number relies on the answer.

prompt: Is Obelisk Bio's 2024 kinase screening dataset clean enough to train the new activity model on? It's one table in the warehouse, so hopefully this is quick. The plates were run in Cambridge, in San Diego, and at the CRO in Shanghai, and each site kept its own deviation log, instrument calibration records and notebook conventions for flagging bad plates.
why: Sounds like one table to inspect, but cleanliness depends on three separate sites' deviation logs, calibration records and flagging conventions, each a long independent investigation.

prompt: Nettlebay ran three usability studies on checkout last year: guest checkout, saved payment methods, and the address form. Checkout has been rebuilt since. Do the findings still hold? Each report has somewhere between 25 and 40 findings, and design wants a still true, fixed, or made worse call on every one because they're retiring the old research deck after this.
why: Only three studies, but that is roughly a hundred findings each needing its own check against the rebuilt flow, and the old deck gets retired on the strength of the result.

prompt: Write the one-pager on why sellers leave Nettlebay for the offsite. Keep it tight, one page. Nobody has ever pulled this together. What we have is the cancellation survey open text, about 30 churn interviews tagged in Dovetail, the seller support queue, and whatever account managers type into Salesforce when a big shop leaves.
why: Looks like a single short writing task, but the content must first be dug out of four unsynthesized sources that each need independent reading before anything can be written.

prompt: Facilities needs the -80 in room 214 emptied by Friday, so we're discarding what's left of Obelisk Bio's ABX-12 aliquots. Can you just confirm nothing still needs them? The program was shut down in 2024. Some material went to two academic collaborators under MTAs, there was a stability study feeding the IND annual report, and a few people pulled samples for side projects that probably only exist on their ELN pages.
why: Phrased as a quick confirmation, but destruction is irreversible and the dependents are an unknown set spread across MTAs, regulatory commitments and individual ELN pages.

prompt: After the July tracking plan change, which of Nettlebay's saved Amplitude cohorts are now quietly wrong? There are 64 of them and lifecycle emails target off most of them. Some events were renamed, a few were split in two, and a couple kept their name but started firing at a different point in the flow.
why: Sounds like something a query over cohort definitions answers, but deciding whether each cohort still means what its owner intended after renames, splits and semantic changes is a separate judgment per cohort.

prompt: Quick one: Obelisk Bio's redesigned LIMS goes to the bench next month. Can you check we didn't drop any screen or field people actually rely on? The old app has no usage tracking. What people really use shows up in the SOPs of the four lab groups, in the validation scripts QA runs for the GxP audit, and in the training decks each group made for new hires.
why: Offhand phrasing suggests a quick diff, but with no usage data the set of relied-on screens must be discovered across four groups' SOPs, QA validation scripts and training material, and a validated system depends on it.

prompt: The deck for Thursday says OB-117 'showed no liver toxicity signal in any preclinical study.' Just make sure that's accurate. For context, tox was split between our in vivo group, two different CROs, and the hepatocyte work the Basel team did before we acquired them.
why: One sentence to verify, but 'any preclinical study' spans four independent bodies of work in different formats and organizations, each needing its own read, and an investor-facing claim depends on it.

prompt: Nettlebay's ML team says the offline gains from our last four search ranking launches carried over online. Can you check that before I put it in the planning doc? Each launch has its own offline eval notebook, its own experiment in Eppo and a launch doc, and two of them ran during holiday traffic, one of those overlapping a search UI change.
why: Only four launches, but each requires reconstructing its offline metric, its online experiment and its confounders independently, which is several long unrelated investigations.

prompt: A Nettlebay buyer filed a deletion request and it's now a regulator complaint. Engineering ran the account deletion job. Can you just confirm the product and research side is clean too? She's been a customer six years and we've switched tools twice in that time. At minimum she was in Amplitude, FullStory replays, a Qualtrics survey and a moderated interview in Dovetail, and analysts sometimes pull user-level exports into Drive.
why: Reads as a single confirmation, but the places her data lives are an open set across current and retired tools plus ad hoc exports, and we must state in writing to a regulator that it is gone.

prompt: Write the methods section for Obelisk Bio's organoid paper. Results are drafted already. Four people ran the experiments over two years, and the culture conditions, passage numbers, imaging settings and analysis parameters are in their own ELN pages, the confocal's acquisition metadata, and a few R scripts in personal repos. Some of it changed partway through.
why: Looks like one document to write, but the facts must be recovered from four people's records, instrument metadata and scattered scripts, including mid-study changes, before a single accurate sentence can be written.

prompt: Pull the adverse events in Obelisk Bio's Phase 1 safety database that were coded to the wrong MedDRA term, before the DSUR goes out. There are 312 events, each with the investigator's verbatim text and a narrative.
why: 'Pull' sounds like a database query, but whether each coding is wrong is a clinical judgment against each verbatim and narrative, repeated 312 times, for a regulatory report.

prompt: The FDA inspector arrives Thursday and wants every Obelisk Bio sample that sat above -70C for more than two hours in the last three years. We cannot miss a single one, a miss becomes a 483 observation. That's 41 freezers across two sites and roughly 180,000 samples. The freezer monitoring system writes each unit's temperature every minute into the same Postgres the LIMS uses, and the LIMS keeps full location history for every sample.
why: Stakes and scale suggest a sweep, but temperature logs and sample location history sit in one database, so a single join over time windows is complete by construction.

prompt: I need Nettlebay's Q3 active seller number exactly right for the board. It shows up in Looker, Sigma, the exec Slack digest, the investor dashboard and the metrics page in Notion, and people keep quoting slightly different figures. Go through all of them. For what it's worth, all five read from fct_active_sellers in dbt, and the Slack digest and Notion page are snapshots taken on whatever day someone last refreshed them.
why: Five surfaces with conflicting numbers look like a multi-source reconciliation, but they all mirror one dbt model, so one query for Q3 gives the answer and snapshot timing explains the drift.

prompt: Nobody knows which of the 230 components in Nettlebay's design system are actually used. They're spread over something like 400 product files and nobody wants to open each one. I need the unused ones so we can cut them before the v3 library. We're on Figma Enterprise with library analytics turned on for the org.
why: 'Nobody knows' and 400 files suggest per-file discovery, but Figma library analytics already reports usage for every component across the org in one view.

prompt: Lay out Obelisk Bio's go/no-go screen for next week: 312 compounds across four 96-well plates. Every plate needs its positive and negative controls, compounds stay out of edge wells where possible, and none of the 14 analog series can land entirely on one plate. Every compound matters here, this screen decides whether the program continues.
why: Many compounds and high stakes invite splitting, but a plate layout is one constraint problem where every well assignment affects the others, so it must be solved in one pass.

prompt: Since Tuesday Nettlebay's Android checkout conversion is down 9%, average order value dipped, payment failed tickets tripled, the seller payouts dashboard shows fewer orders and the fraud team's decline rate chart spiked. Five teams, five dashboards, dig into each one. Android 7.4 with the new payments SDK went to 100% of users Tuesday at 10am, which is exactly when all five lines move.
why: Five teams and five alarms look like independent investigations, but they share one onset at one release, so this is a single causal chain from the payments SDK outward.

prompt: Spin up a bunch of agents in parallel to compute IC50s for the 40 compounds in this plate reader export. Same four-parameter logistic fit for every compound, same normalization to the plate controls, and I want them all in one table.
why: The user asks for parallel agents, but it is one deterministic curve-fitting script run over a single file.

prompt: Before we reuse old interview recordings in the brand film, Legal wants every Nettlebay research participant who has withdrawn consent since 2022. Every single one, showing someone who opted out would be a real problem. We've run around 900 sessions. Recruiting has handled all consent through User Interviews since 2021, logs every withdrawal on the participant record there, and it exports.
why: Completeness language and 900 sessions suggest a hunt, but consent withdrawals have one authoritative system of record with an export, so one pull is the complete list.

prompt: We ran a full factorial DoE on Obelisk Bio's new binding assay: cell density, incubation time, antibody concentration and wash count, two levels each, in triplicate. The plate data is all in one CSV. I want a proper look at each of the four factors so we can lock the protocol.
why: Four factors each wanting 'a proper look' reads like four separate analyses, but a factorial design is analyzed as one model with interactions, and per-factor conclusions made separately would be wrong.
